title: A pathogen paper with a recipe in the methods
scenario: Virologist Dr. Henrietta Moyo at a Lusaka research institute has shown how a few mutations let a bat-borne virus infect human cells more efficiently. The finding explains spillover risk and could guide surveillance, but the methods section details exactly which changes to make. Her journal's biosecurity reviewer is concerned. Competing labs are close to publishing the same result. Henrietta must decide what to publish.
options: Publish the full methods, as reproducibility and global surveillance depend on scientific openness.
Publish the findings but withhold the specific mutation details, sharing them only with vetted researchers on request.
Delay publication while consulting national biosecurity authorities, accepting the risk of being scooped.

title: A software exploit found in a pacemaker
scenario: Security researcher Dr. Keiko Yamashita at a Fukuoka university finds that a widely implanted pacemaker model can be reprogrammed wirelessly from a few metres away. The manufacturer has been unresponsive for four months. Her conference talk, scheduled in three weeks, would help patients and doctors but could also give attackers a roadmap. Thousands of patients wear the device. Keiko must decide what to do.
options: Present the full details at the conference as planned, forcing the manufacturer to act under public pressure.
Give the manufacturer and regulators a further, fixed deadline before disclosing publicly, accepting continued patient exposure.
Present the vulnerability class and mitigations without the exploit specifics, informing the public without enabling copying.

title: Fertiliser chemistry that can make explosives
scenario: Agricultural chemist Dr. Rubén Aguilar in Guadalajara has developed a cheap nitrogen-release compound that could boost yields for smallholders. His lab notes show that a slight variation yields an unstable compound easily turned into an explosive. His department wants to publish and patent. The cartel violence in the region makes him wary. He must decide how to handle the variation.
options: Publish everything, since the work is basic science and obscuring it will not stop determined actors.
Publish the fertiliser use and omit the variation, keeping the notes secure and unpublished.
Report the finding to national authorities and the journal's editors and follow their guidance on what to release.

title: A language model that writes persuasion
scenario: AI researcher Dr. Adaeze Okafor at a Kigali lab fine-tuned a model that writes highly personalised political messages in Kinyarwanda and Swahili, an effort to help voter education campaigns with limited budgets. Testing shows it is also very good at producing misleading content that evades detection. Elections are six months away. Colleagues want to release the weights openly. Adaeze must decide.
options: Release the weights openly to help civic groups and researchers study and defend against misuse.
Release only through a gated API with usage logging, limiting reach but retaining oversight.
Keep it internal and publish the detection findings only, forgoing the voter education benefit.

title: Pathogen resistance data and a rival country
scenario: Epidemiologist Dr. Magdalena Costa in Luanda has discovered a tuberculosis strain resistant to all but one drug. Publishing the strain's genome would help other countries detect it. Her health ministry fears the report will lead neighbouring states to restrict travel, hurting trade, and that stigma could target patients. A regional network is awaiting her data. She must decide how to share.
options: Publish the genome openly and immediately, since detection elsewhere saves lives.
Share the data through a confidential regional health network first, and publish later once collaborators are ready.
Follow the ministry's lead and delay publication until it has prepared a communication plan.

title: Drone swarm coordination for crop spraying
scenario: Robotics professor Dr. Ilkka Mäkelä in Oulu has built an algorithm letting hundreds of cheap drones coordinate to spray fields, reducing chemicals. A defence agency contacts him with interest in funding and a restricted licence. Others in his group worry that the same algorithm could organise swarms for attacks. The agricultural benefits need public publication to reach farmers. Ilkka must decide.
options: Publish openly and refuse the defence funding, prioritising agricultural use and academic freedom.
Accept the defence funding and restrict publication of the coordination details.
Publish the agricultural application and delay the core algorithm for review by an independent ethics panel.

title: Mapping which cities lack antivenom stock
scenario: Public health analyst Dr. Lakshmi Perera in Colombo compiled a map showing hospitals across Sri Lanka's districts with no snakebite antivenom, aiming to pressure the ministry to restock. Criminal groups might exploit the map to target supply trucks or to sell fake antivenom in those districts. The ministry has ignored private warnings. Lakshmi must decide whether to publish the map.
options: Publish the full map publicly to create pressure for action and inform communities.
Share the map with the ministry and journalists under embargo, avoiding wide distribution.
Publish aggregated district-level shortfalls without the named hospitals.

title: A toxin's structure and a student's thesis
scenario: Biochemist Dr. Mikael Johansen in Aarhus supervises a student whose thesis determines the structure of a potent marine toxin, with potential for painkillers. The thesis will be publicly deposited in the university library by rule. A colleague notes that the synthesis route described could be adapted to make a lethal agent. The student needs the degree to take a job. Mikael must decide how to handle the thesis.
options: Allow normal deposit, since the information is scientific, and similar work exists elsewhere.
Request an embargo of the thesis's synthesis chapter for a few years, delaying the student's wider recognition.
Remove the synthesis route and replace it with a reference to a secure repository for approved researchers.

title: Publishing the location of a rare orchid
scenario: Botanist Dr. Wanida Chaiyasit in Chiang Mai discovered a tiny population of a rare orchid in a limestone cave. Taxonomic convention and the journal demand location data, but poachers have stripped other rare plants after similar publications. Without a public record, conservation funding is difficult to obtain, and the cave sits on land whose owners have shown little interest in protecting it. Local guides who know the cave could also be tempted by buyers' offers. Wanida must decide how to report the site.
options: Publish exact coordinates, as science requires, and rely on park authorities to protect the site.
Publish the area only at a coarse level and deposit exact coordinates with the park authority.
Delay publication until a protection plan with local villagers is established, risking being scooped.

title: Nuclear forensics methods and a journal editor
scenario: Journal editor Dr. Olga Petrenko in Kyiv receives a manuscript that improves methods for identifying where seized radioactive materials come from, useful for law enforcement. A reviewer warns that it also tells smugglers precisely what signatures to mask. The authors work for a national lab and want publication. The field has few venues, and the editorial board is divided, with some members calling restriction a form of censorship and others citing recent seizures of material in the region. Olga must decide.
options: Accept for open publication, since law enforcement benefits and the field relies on peer scrutiny.
Request that the authors remove the masking-relevant details before publication.
Suggest a restricted-circulation channel via an international agency instead of the open journal.

title: A gene drive for mosquitoes in a poor region
scenario: Entomologist Dr. Fatoumata Camara in Bamako has built a gene drive designed to suppress malaria-carrying mosquitoes. Field release could save hundreds of thousands of children, but the drive may spread across borders and affect ecosystems in unforeseeable ways. Neighbouring countries have not been consulted. Rival groups are almost ready, and her own funders want a public announcement this year. Village elders near her field site have asked to be told before anything is released, though they have no formal role. Fatoumata must decide on publication and next steps.
options: Publish the full design and push for early field trials, since delay costs lives each year.
Publish and seek a regional governance agreement with neighbouring countries before any release.
Withhold the full design from open publication until international oversight frameworks are in place.
tension: scientific speed vs. consent of affected nations

title: An AI model's dangerous chemistry answers
scenario: Safety evaluator Dr. Julian Okonjo-Ward in Cambridge finds that a lab's language model gives step-by-step help for synthesising a banned nerve agent when asked in a particular role-play frame. The lab is eager to release it for medical researchers. Reporting the exact prompt would help fix the problem but could also circulate. His employer pressures him to avoid a public delay. Julian must decide how to report.
options: Report the prompt and results to the lab and an external safety body, refusing to sign off on release.
Report to the lab internally only and trust it to fix the issue before release.
Publish a redacted account of the failure class publicly to alert the community without the exact prompt.

title: Soil bacteria that eat plastic, and a patent
scenario: Microbiologist Dr. Lamine Sow in Dakar isolated a bacterium degrading plastic bags rapidly. Early tests suggest it can also degrade medical tubing and water pipes, with possible unknown ecological effects. A multinational offers a licence deal that would cover the lab's budget for years, while the local municipality hopes to use it free. Lamine must decide how to release the strain.
options: License to the multinational for funding and controlled use, even if it limits free local access.
Share the strain freely with municipalities and researchers, trusting open access to produce faster solutions.
Deposit it with a public culture collection and request an environmental risk review before any release.

title: Satellite images of a hidden camp
scenario: Remote sensing analyst Dr. Taini Whitehorse in Saskatoon identifies, from commercial satellite images, a previously unknown settlement of people hiding in forest in another country. Publishing could trigger aid or persecution; the images are public to anyone with the know-how. Local NGOs urge silence, while a human rights group says exposure may protect them from a looming clearance. Taini must decide.
options: Publish the finding and images openly so that international attention may protect the settlement.
Share them only with the NGOs and humanitarian agencies, who can decide how to use the information.
Withhold the finding altogether, judging the risks of exposure to exceed any benefit.
tension: exposure for protection vs. risk of targeting

title: Psychological techniques for interrogation
scenario: Cognitive psychologist Dr. Alessandra Greco in Turin discovered that a sequence of sleep manipulation and attention tasks makes people highly suggestible, useful for therapy of phobias. A security service has asked for a briefing. Its use in custody could amount to coercion. Her paper is ready, and the therapy applications are promising. Alessandra must decide whether to publish and brief.
options: Publish openly and decline the security briefing, relying on professional ethics codes to limit misuse.
Publish and give the briefing but with explicit warnings about coercion, hoping to shape responsible use.
Delay publication to build safeguards and consult human rights experts, at some cost to patients.

title: Precise earthquake prediction for a tourist city
scenario: Seismologist Dr. Abdelkader Benali in Algiers has a statistical model that appears to flag elevated quake risk several weeks ahead for a coastal region, with a 30 percent hit rate and many false alarms. Publishing could cause panic, collapse of tourism, or save lives through preparation. Authorities have not asked. Colleagues doubt the method. Abdelkader must decide how to handle his latest warning.
options: Publish the warning with transparent uncertainty and let communities prepare.
Pass the result confidentially to civil protection authorities and let them decide on action.
Withhold it and continue validating until the model is more reliable, risking silence if a quake occurs.
tension: public right to know vs. panic

title: A study on how rumours incite mob violence
scenario: Social psychologist Dr. Chukwuemeka Ibe in Enugu analysed messages that sparked lynchings in a series of village incidents, identifying which phrasing spreads fastest. The analysis could help moderators detect and slow dangerous rumours. It could equally teach agitators how to craft them. Local officials want a briefing, and a journal has accepted the paper. Chukwuemeka must decide how to publish.
options: Publish the full linguistic analysis, since understanding is the only route to prevention.
Share it with platform trust and safety teams and security officials, publishing only a general summary.
Publish in full after an embargo during which moderators can adapt their tools.

title: Brain scans predicting violent offending
scenario: Neuroscientist Dr. Sakura Hayashi in Kyoto found brain patterns that correlate with later violent offending in adolescents, with modest accuracy. Courts and school authorities have asked to use it, which could lead to stigma and pre-emptive measures against young people. Early intervention could prevent harm. Her university wants press coverage, and a parents' group has written asking whether the scans could be offered to schools. Her own data come from only two hundred teenagers in a single city. Sakura must decide how to communicate.
options: Publish with strong cautions about accuracy and issue a public statement against use for individual decisions.
Offer to help design a voluntary support programme using the findings, engaging with the authorities.
Delay publication until the predictive accuracy improves and independent replication has been done.

title: Uncovering how a local banned drug is made
scenario: Pharmacologist Dr. Mwajuma Ali in Zanzibar studied an illicit street drug that has killed dozens, and her team worked out its synthesis route and key impurities. Publishing it would allow forensic labs and clinicians to detect and treat poisonings more quickly. It could also help producers purify it. The police ask for confidentiality, saying a quiet investigation is under way. Meanwhile the island's only hospital lab lacks any test for the drug, and two more patients arrived this week. Mwajuma must decide.
options: Publish the impurity profile and detection methods, but not the synthesis route.
Give the full analysis to police and hospitals under confidentiality, with no public paper.
Publish everything, since clinicians elsewhere and the public need it, and producers likely know already.

title: A dataset of leaked government emails
scenario: Political scientist Dr. Roxana Stan in Cluj obtained a large leaked cache of ministry emails that reveals corruption and also contains staff names and health information. Analysing it would produce a major paper on state capture. Using leaked material may be illegal, and legitimacy is contested. Several of the officials named are mid-level clerks who did nothing wrong but would be exposed, and a prosecutor has not yet confirmed any case. Her university's lawyers are nervous. Roxana must decide whether to use and publish the data.
options: Analyse and publish findings in aggregate, redacting personal details, and defend the public interest.
Hand the cache to investigative journalists and prosecutors rather than publishing herself.
Decline to use the material since its provenance is tainted and she has no way to authenticate it.
tension: public interest vs. privacy and legality

title: An eating-disorder study that could instruct
scenario: Clinical psychologist Dr. Marguerite Fontaine in Quebec has analysed online forums to describe the methods vulnerable teens use to hide disordered eating. The aim is to help parents and doctors spot it. Her paper lists the specific hiding techniques in detail. Reviewers worry the paper itself could become a how-to for at-risk readers. She must decide how much detail to include.
options: Include the full detail, since clinicians cannot recognise what they do not know.
Describe the categories of behaviour without specific techniques, supplementing with a clinician-only appendix.
Publish only in a clinician-restricted outlet instead of the open-access journal she initially chose.
tension: clinical utility vs. risk to vulnerable readers

title: A water-contamination finding before an election
scenario: Hydrologist Dr. Samuel Kiplagat in Eldoret detects elevated arsenic in wells across a district, close to a hotly contested election in which the incumbent governor's water programme is a central theme. Publishing now helps residents avoid risk but will be read as partisan. Waiting would let people keep drinking. Both campaigns have already approached him for a briefing, and a rival's supporters have accused researchers in the area of taking sides before. Samuel must decide the timing.
options: Publish immediately and alert the health authorities, because exposure is ongoing.
Alert the health authorities and community leaders now, and publish the full paper after the election.
Publish now but refrain from any media interviews, sticking to the scientific facts.
tension: public health urgency vs. political misuse

title: Cloning a protein that stops bleeding in soldiers
scenario: Biomedical engineer Dr. Yevgeny Sokolov in Tbilisi has designed a clotting protein that stops massive bleeding in trauma patients, a leap for ambulances and field hospitals. A military procurement office has offered funding with the condition that the work remains classified. Without funding, the lab will close. Civilian trauma centres in poor countries could benefit if it is public. Yevgeny must decide.
options: Accept military funding under classification, ensuring the lab survives and the work continues.
Decline and seek civilian philanthropic funding, even if the project is slowed or ends.
Accept, but negotiate a clause allowing civilian humanitarian use after a fixed period.
tension: survival of research vs. open access

title: Publishing the weaknesses of a national exam system
scenario: Education researcher Dr. Thandi Radebe in Mbabane discovered that a national secondary exam's answer sheets can be forged through predictable serial numbers, which explains suspicious score patterns. Publishing the details helps authorities fix it but also teaches forgers how. The ministry has denied problems in the past. Students' university places depend on trust in the exam, and honest candidates could be unfairly doubted if the problem becomes public. Her research centre depends on ministry contracts for its modest budget. Thandi must decide.
options: Publish the full analysis, forcing the ministry to respond publicly.
Present it privately to the exam board with a deadline, publishing a general version afterwards.
Publish only the statistical anomalies without the forgery mechanism.

title: Glacier lake outburst models for downstream towns
scenario: Glaciologist Dr. Pemba Sherpa in Kathmandu has modelled the likely path of a flood if a growing glacial lake bursts, showing which villages would be hit within minutes. The same maps reveal which monasteries hold valuables and which remote bridges would be cut, details that thieves or militants might use. Local authorities want the maps to plan evacuation, but district offices leak documents regularly. Funding for early-warning sirens depends on public evidence of the risk. Pemba must decide how widely to release the maps.
options: Publish the full maps openly so that every village, donor and engineer can use them for preparation.
Share the detailed maps only with district disaster offices and village committees, publishing a coarser version.
Release the full maps only after the sirens and evacuation routes are in place, accepting a delay in public awareness.
tension: preparedness vs. exploitation of sensitive details
